title: Quantization impact digest — AWQ / GPTQ / int8 / int4 (working)
content:
Objective:
Summarize observed quality deltas when converting the onboarding candidate model (Llama-2-13B-chat baseline) to four quantization formats: int8 (per-channel symmetric), int4 (GPTQ-style with group size 128), AWQ-optimized int4, and GPTQ float->4bit. This doc is a working digest intended to capture per-slice deltas, significance signals, and actionable recommendations for the model onboarding checklist.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- AWQ-int4 shows the best cost/quality tradeoff across most conversational/instruction slices: median relative loss on primary instruction-following metric ~0.8–1.4% absolute (small).
- GPTQ-int4 (our current fast-path) shows slightly higher delta, with pronounced regressions on math and long-context reasoning slices (~3.5–6% abs).
- int8 has negligible impact on generation quality (<0.4% across most slices) and is a safe default for Dedicated deployments when latency/cost is not strictly limited.
- int4 (naive quant) produced large regressions on code and tabular reasoning slices; do not promote to production without slice-specific mitigation.
- Several slices show heterogeneous behavior (e.g., hallucination rate decreases on short-qa but increases on long-qa for AWQ).

Why this matters:
Onboarding requires both a unit-cost story and per-slice quality guarantees. Product teams have SLOs defined on top of metric baskets (instr-f1, exact-match, hallucination-rate). Small average losses can hide large regressions on narrow but critical slices (safety-related, billing/legal text). This digest flags slices needing targeted evals before rolling out quantized variants.

Models & artifacts evaluated:
- base: Llama-2-13B-chat (hf id: Llama2-13b-chat-final)
- variants: base-int8-sym, base-int4-gptq-gs128, base-awq-int4-opt, base-gptq-4bit
- eval harness: internal/eval-harness v0.9.2 (deterministic generation: top-p=0.95, temp=0.0 for scoring; sampling runs for human-like metrics at temp=0.7)
- prompt sets: onboarding/pset-v2 (combined: instruction, code, math, long-context, safety)
- eval date: 2025-02-02

Methodology (short):
- Metric baskets: instruction-F1 (token overlap), exact-match (EM) for QA, code-pass@1 (execution), rougeL for summarization, hallucination-rate (human-labeled subset), and perplexity on held-out tokens.
- For each slice and quant format we ran N=1000 prompts (where feasible) stratified by length and difficulty; for code we ran 2000 code prompts to get stable pass@1.
- Report absolute metric deltas (quant - base) and relative percent where helpful. We report two-sided bootstrap 95% CIs (1000 resamples).
- Flag slices where the absolute EM/F1 loss > 2.0 points or p-value < 0.05 (bootstrap) as high-priority regressions.

Slice definitions and sizes (sampled):
- instr-short (n=1500): one-shot, user instructions < 80 tokens; typical product prompts.
- instr-long (n=800): multi-step instructions, > 250 tokens with tool calls.
- code-python (n=2000): function writing + unit tests (pass@1 execution).
- math-arith (n=700): arithmetic and algebra chain-of-thought style problems.
- long-context (n=1200): prompts requiring >4096 token context (summaries, refactoring).
- knowledge-recall (n=1000): factual QA requiring lookup-style recall.
- table-reason (n=600): reasoning over structured CSV-like inputs.
- safety-sensitive (n=400): adversarial prompts measuring hallucination and refusal.

Key quantitative results (high level):
(Notes: all deltas shown are quant_variant - base; positive means quant is better.)
- int8 (per-channel symmetric): mean delta EM/F1 across slices = -0.12 points (95% CI [-0.38, +0.09]) — effectively neutral. Hallucination-rate delta +0.6% (not significant).
- GPTQ-int4: mean delta = -1.6 points (95% CI [-2.7, -0.9]). Large regressions on math-arith (-4.1 abs EM), long-context (-3.5 abs rougeL), code-python (-5.2% pass@1).
- AWQ-int4: mean delta = -0.9 points (95% CI [-1.8, -0.3]). Code-python down -1.9% pass@1 (better than GPTQ), math-arith -2.4 EM. Long-context shows mixed signal: rougeL -1.0 (CI includes 0).
- Naive int4: mean delta = -3.9 points (95% CI [-5.4, -2.6]) — clear quality regressions across almost all slices.

Per-slice highlights (selected):
- code-python: base pass@1 = 71.4%; int8 = 70.9% (-0.5 abs); AWQ-int4 = 69.5% (-1.9); GPTQ-int4 = 66.2% (-5.2); naive-int4 = 60.7% (-10.7).
- math-arith: base EM = 64.2%; int8 = 63.9 (-0.3); AWQ-int4 = 61.8 (-2.4); GPTQ-int4 = 60.1 (-4.1); naive-int4 = 55.0 (-9.2).
- long-context: base rougeL = 41.3; int8 = 41.0 (-0.3); AWQ-int4 = 40.3 (-1.0); GPTQ-int4 = 37.8 (-3.5); naive-int4 = 34.9 (-6.4).
- safety-sensitive: base hallucination-rate = 6.1%; int8 = 6.7 (+0.6); AWQ-int4 = 7.4 (+1.3); GPTQ-int4 = 8.9 (+2.8). Note: the safety slice shows higher hallucination increases for aggressive 4-bit quant.

Statistical notes:
- We used bootstrap CIs and permutation tests for significance; where sample sizes were small (safety-sensitive, n=400) confidence intervals are wide — interpret with caution.
- For pass@1 we applied Clopper-Pearson intervals since outcomes are binary.
- Multiple comparisons: we applied Benjamini-Hochberg correction within each metric family (e.g., all EM tests together) to control FDR.

Qualitative observations from human-in-the-loop review (Lina, Miguel):
- AWQ tends to preserve surface-form answers (short instruction/completion) but sometimes omits intermediate reasoning steps — leads to lower chain-of-thought fidelity on math prompts.
- GPTQ-int4 truncates or collapses long token dependencies more often, causing long-context regeneration drift.
- Code failures under GPTQ-int4 are often deterministic syntax errors (missing import lines or truncated function signatures) — suggests per-layer bias introduced by group-wise quantization.

Cost / perf tradeoffs (rough):
- int8: ~1.8x speedup vs fp16 in our dedicated-pool benchmark, cost delta ~-22% per token.
- AWQ-int4: ~3.6x speedup, cost delta ~-48% per token.
- GPTQ-int4: ~3.9x speedup, cost delta ~-52% per token.
- naive-int4: similar perf to GPTQ-int4 but worse quality so not worth it.

Recommendations (short):
1) Promote int8 variant to Dedicated onboarding as default safe-quant. Low risk, minimal quality delta.
2) Promote AWQ-int4 to a staged canary for hosted API on select customers and non-safety-critical routes. Monitor code and math slices closely.
3) Hold GPTQ-int4 from broad production use until we can: (a) re-run with group-size tuning (try GS=32,64), (b) test layer-wise calibration fixes used in prior PRs.
4) Avoid naive int4 for any customer-facing workload.
5) Add slice-level rollout gates: require pass@1 delta <= 2.0 points for code routes and EM delta <= 1.5 for math/qa routes before defaulting to 4-bit.

Immediate next steps / action items (owner):
- Run reproducibility pass with different random seeds for GPTQ-int4 and AWQ-int4 (Asha) — due 2025-02-10.
- Investigate GPTQ group-size sweep (Lina + infra) and re-evaluate code slice (due 2025-02-17). Link to job: JIRA-ML-6142.
- Prepare a canary rollout plan for AWQ-int4 for Hosted (Devon) including per-route opt-in and telemetry dashboards (due 2025-02-20).
- Add per-slice alerting in Redwood Console for runbook thresholds (SRE/Console team).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How does AWQ perform on instruction-following when using sampling decodes (we used mostly argmax for EM scoring)? Need to re-run sampling-based metrics.
- Are there decoder-layer-specific patterns we can use to selectively dequantize hot layers to recover code pass@1 without full fp16 cost? (Research task)
- Would group-size tuning for GPTQ close >50% of observed deficits? Early experiments suggest some improvement but not enough data yet.

Appendix: quick provenance & reproducibility notes:
- Eval harness commit: git@github.com:redwood-inference/model-evals@91f4b7c
- Quant conversion scripts: tools/quantize/{awq_convert.py,gptq_run.sh}
- Random seeds used: [42, 1024, 2025] across replicates.
- Full per-prompt CSVs (scored outputs + logits) saved to internal bucket: gs://redwood-evals/quant/2025-02-02/ — request access via the ML Slack channel.

If you want a short slide deck of these findings for the onboarding review, I can draft 3 slides focusing on (1) headline deltas, (2) per-slice waterfall for code & math, (3) rollout plan.

Notes to self: keep this doc as the working single source for quant onboarding; once canaries complete, produce a final report (status: final) and copy export to Confluence.
